profile.reading:
This Lumen facility is located in the Madison, Wisconsin area of Dane County, at coordinates that place it within the city itself rather than in one of Dane County's surrounding suburbs or rural townships. No confirmed street address for this specific building was located in this pass, only its geographic coordinates, so no address is stated here beyond the city and county already on file for this record.

The operator is Lumen Technologies, the telecommunications company that traces its lineage through a series of mergers, CenturyLink's 2011 acquisition of Qwest Communications, itself a descendant of the old US West regional Bell operating company that served much of the upper Midwest including Wisconsin, and CenturyLink's 2017 merger with Level 3 Communications, before the combined company rebranded itself Lumen Technologies in 2020. A facility named as a discrete Lumen data center in a state capital and university city like Madison is consistent with the pattern of a legacy incumbent local exchange carrier central office or regional network hub, a building originally built or adapted to house telephone switching equipment for the surrounding metro area and later repurposed or expanded for colocation and interconnection services as demand for that kind of space grew, though no public building permit, Dane County property record, or architectural history specific to this address was located in this pass to confirm that reading for this particular building.

Lumen does not publish site specific technical details for individual colocation locations on its public marketing pages. The company's own site describes its overall North American colocation footprint as more than 200 locations across more than 120 cities, serving more than 2,600 colocation customers, with cabinet and cage based space offered at power densities from roughly 3 kW to 12 kW, AC and DC power delivery options, N, 2N, and N+1 cooling and generator redundancy configurations depending on the site, and a network operations center monitoring the portfolio around the clock. Lumen states that more than 50 of its locations carry compliance certifications, without naming which ones, and advertises a 100 percent uptime service level commitment across its colocation portfolio. None of these figures are broken out by individual site, so no capacity, redundancy tier, or certification status specific to the Madison location is recorded here, and none of Lumen's IT capacity, utility power, or generator figures for this address specifically were found in public sourcing.

Madison sits outside the major hyperscale data center corridors that have grown up around cheap hydropower in places like central Washington, or around fiber and land availability in northern Virginia, and functions instead as a regional network point of presence supporting Dane County's state government, University of Wisconsin, and mixed commercial economy. No trade press coverage naming this specific Madison facility, and no Wisconsin state or Dane County government record referencing it individually, was found in this pass.

reading.body:
Lumen Madison 1 is a single building colocation facility in Wisconsin's state capital, operated by Lumen Technologies as part of its 200-location North American network of regional interconnection hubs. Lumen publishes no IT load, utility power capacity, or technical specifications for this specific address, only aggregate portfolio figures stating that its colocation sites range from roughly 3 kW to 12 kW per cabinet and carry various redundancy tiers, with more than 50 of its locations holding compliance certifications without naming which ones.

The facility likely traces its origins to the telephone network infrastructure legacy of US West and its successors through Qwest and Level 3 Communications, serving Madison's metro area as a regional switching and network hub before its repurposing for colocation services, though no building record confirming this history was found. Madison sits outside the major hyperscale data center corridors that have concentrated AI compute around cheap power and fiber in places like central Washington and northern Virginia, functioning instead as a mid-tier point of presence for state government, the University of Wisconsin, and regional commercial demand.

Wisconsin published capacity stands at 1.6 MW across all mapped facilities with disclosed figures, ranking this facility second in the state by published capacity, though that ranking reflects only the one facility in Wisconsin that publishes a specific MW figure at all. The facility carries no published nameplate capacity, so its actual share of Wisconsin's AI-relevant infrastructure cannot be calculated from available sources, and no local or trade press coverage naming this specific Madison location as a current AI or accelerator deployment site was found.
